concept.name: Wash trading
concept.definition: Entering into, or purporting to enter into, transactions that give the appearance that purchases and sales have been made without incurring market risk or changing the trader's market position; the Commodity Exchange Act prohibits wash trading, and Section 9(a)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 prohibits transactions involving no change in beneficial ownership (and matched orders) done to create a false or misleading appearance of active trading.
concept.intuition: You sell to yourself — the asset never really changes hands and you take no risk, but the tape lights up with 'activity' that lures in real traders.
concept.mechanics: The same beneficial owner (or colluding parties) acts as both buyer and seller, often across accounts or venues, generating fictitious volume and prices. Because no genuine change of ownership or risk occurs, the printed trades convey false information about liquidity and interest in the instrument.
concept.failure_modes: Self-trades can occur accidentally at firms running multiple algorithms, and bona fide transfers between accounts for legitimate purposes can resemble wash trades; regulators look for intent, repetition, and absence of economic rationale, and exchanges generally require systems to prevent self-match.
concept.misconceptions: Wash trading (a manipulation offense) is different from the tax wash-sale rule (a loss-disallowance rule); also, a trade between two accounts at the same institution is not automatically a wash trade — the key is no change in beneficial ownership plus manipulative purpose.
concept.example: A crypto trader controls two exchange accounts and repeatedly sells tokens between them at rising prices, inflating reported volume to attract momentum buyers to an illiquid token.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Section 9(a), 15 U.S.C. § 78i (U.S. Code, GPO)
